data.title: Fetal behavior during MRI changes with age and relates to network dynamics

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9921243, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Fetal motor behavior is an important clinical indicator of healthy development. However, our understanding of associations between fetal behavior and fetal brain development is limited. To fill this gap, this study introduced an approach to automatically and objectively classify long durations of fetal movement from a continuous four‐dimensional functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data set, and paired behavior features with brain activity indicated by the fMRI time series. Twelve‐minute fMRI scans were conducted in 120 normal fetuses. Postnatal motor function was evaluated at 7 and 36 months age. Fetal motor behavior was quantified by calculating the frame‐wise displacement (FD) of fetal brains extracted by a deep‐learning model along the whole time series. Analyzing only low motion data, we characterized the recurring coactivation patterns (CAPs) of the supplementary motor area (SMA). Results showed reduced motor activity with advancing gestational age (GA), likely due in part to loss of space (r = −.51, p < .001). Evaluation of individual variation in motor movement revealed a negative association between movement and the occurrence of coactivations within the left parietotemporal network, controlling for age and sex (p = .003). Further, we found that the occurrence of coactivations between the SMA to posterior brain regions, including visual cortex, was prospectively associated with postnatal motor function at 7 months (r = .43, p = .03). This is the first study to pair fetal movement and fMRI, highlighting potential for comparisons of fetal behavior and neural network development to enhance our understanding of fetal brain organization.

data.abstract: Editorial for “A Graph Theory Study of Resting-State Functional MRI Connectivity in Children With Carbon Monoxide Poisoning” Carbon monoxide (CO) is a tasteless, odorless, and colorless nonirritating gas with several nonoccupational sources in common households. Due to the above properties, exposure to CO is of serious health concern, as individuals are usually unaware of the poisoning up until or beyond the point of serious or fatal intoxication. The high toxicity of CO is mainly attributable to its capability to bind to hemoglobin, with nearly 200-fold higher affinity than that of oxygen, leading to general hypoxia. The worldwide cumulative incidence of CO poisoning in 2017 was 137 cases per million, with a mortality of 4.6 deaths per million. However, the incidence ratio is not uniform among age groups; children aged under 5 and between 5 and –9 have the highest incidence ratio, and CO poisoning in children between 0 and 14 accounts for 31% of all cases. Both the acute effects and the treatment protocols of CO poisoning have well-elaborated literature, along with the description of long-term neuropsychiatric and cardiac sequelae. On the other hand, the literature on resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) abnormalities in CO intoxication is rather modest, and this is particularly true regarding the studies of the underaged population, where the rapidly developing brain possibly voids the general findings based on adult samples and limits our comprehensive understanding of the disease. In this issue of JMRI, Liu et al reported on the restingstate functional connectivity alterations in children with CO intoxication. The main purpose of the study was to investigate the topological alterations of the whole-brain connectome in children with CO intoxication and correlate the graph theory measures with disease severity. The authors have enrolled 26 patients (13 females, aged 12.23 2.43) and 26 healthy ageand sex-matched control subjects. Sevenminute-long rs-fMRI data were collected on 3 T scanner and processed with GRETNA toolbox using default preprocessing steps, including slice-time correction, motion correction, MNI normalization, and spatial smoothing with 6 mm FWHM kernel. Linear detrending and bandpass filtering from 0.01 to 0.08 Hz was used along with the scrubbing of frames exceeding 0.5 mm frame-wise displacement. Nodes were determined using both anatomical AAL-90 and functional Dosenbach-160 atlases. Finally, global and regional brain network parameters were calculated, and statistical inferences were assessed between groups. Compared with the normal sample, the authors showed that CO-poisoned children had longer path lengths and reduced global efficiency along with reduced small-worldness (global metrics). Regionally, several regions including the basal ganglia (right thalamus, caudate nucleus, and pallidum) and bilateral hippocampus showed reduced nodal degree, nodal efficiency, and increased shortest path. Besides, authors reported several other regions where opposite change was observed (e.g. left parietal lobe, supplementary motor area, postcentral gyrus, and paracentral lobule). Functional connectivity strength measures identified two altered circuits between the groups, one primarily located in the right frontal lobe and the basal ganglia, the other in the temporal, occipital, and parietal lobes. Network metrics also showed significant associations with clinical indicators: coma time was related to regional network parameters of left orbital and inferior frontal cortices, while COHb% was a significant predictor of the node shortest path of the right Rolandic operculum. Children with CO poisoning showed increased characteristic path length and decreased small-worldness. These findings are in accordance with the clinical observations of neuropsychiatric alterations (disorientation, cognitive impairment, memory loss, etc.) as these global network parameters are often used as a proxy for the degree of network performance: efficiency of information transfer and the ability to properly integrate information, respectively. In addition to the alterations in global network topology, the local (nodal and edge) attributes may point to localized damage, probably in brain areas, or networks that are the most vulnerable to hypoxic insult in children.
